strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely efficiency problem in LVLM inference: visual tokens dominate prefilling cost, especially for high-resolution image and video inputs. A training-free method that can be plugged into existing models is practically valuable.

The proposed two-stage design is simple and sensible: greedy k-center retention encourages spatial/semantic coverage among visual tokens, while later removal of visual tokens based on cross-modal attention ratios targets the observation that deeper LLM layers rely less on visual-token interaction.

The experimental section is relatively broad for an efficiency paper, covering eight image benchmarks and four video benchmarks, two LLaVA-NeXT model sizes, multiple pruning ratios, and several efficiency metrics including FLOPs, memory, throughput, and wall-clock time.

The reported accuracy-efficiency tradeoff is promising: at 10% retained visual tokens, ToDRE maintains higher average image performance than FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, and GlobalCom2, while also improving throughput and memory relative to the uncompressed baseline.

The ablations isolate the two stages and generally support the claim that diversity-based early retention drives most of the speedup, while the relevance-based second stage provides smaller but complementary gains.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. Greedy k-center/diversity-based visual token selection is a natural and established idea, and the paper cites a directly relevant 2025 work, DivPrune: Diversity-based visual token pruning for large multimodal models, but does not compare against it or clearly distinguish the algorithmic contribution from that line beyond adding a second pruning stage.

The theoretical appendix is weak and largely unconvincing. It assumes orthogonal visual and text subspaces and then derives independence/covariance conclusions that do not follow for real LVLM embeddings or attention dynamics. This does not materially support the method and may overstate the theoretical grounding.

The evaluation is broad in benchmarks but narrow in model families: all main experiments use LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B. Claims of architecture-agnostic transfer would be stronger with results on other LVLM families, especially newer or structurally different backbones such as Qwen-VL/InternVL-style models.

The second-stage contribution appears relatively small in practice. Most gains come from Stage 1; Stage 2 changes total time only modestly after Stage 1 and sometimes yields very small or mixed metric changes. The paper should temper claims that Stage 2 is a major source of acceleration except for potentially long-generation settings, which are not quantitatively evaluated.

The claim of excellent compatibility with efficient attention operators is not fully substantiated. The relevance stage requires cross-modal attention probabilities at selected layers, which may conflict with standard FlashAttention-style kernels that avoid materializing attention matrices unless special handling is used. The overhead and implementation details should be made clearer.

Several reporting details reduce confidence: the abstract claims 2.6x speedup while Table 3 reports 1.9x throughput improvement; Table 2 labels the unpruned baseline retain ratio as 0%; and the text discussing Table 4 contains inconsistent timing numbers for the 25% setting. These may be fixable, but they make the empirical presentation feel less polished.

The comparisons omit some relevant recent token pruning/reduction baselines and do not report statistical variability or repeated-run stability. Given that some gains over the strongest baselines are modest on individual benchmarks, variance estimates would help judge robustness.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Key implementation choices such as exact normalization before k-center, overhead accounting for similarity computation, prompt/evaluation settings, and whether code will be released are not sufficiently detailed.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely efficiency problem in LVLM inference, where visual tokens dominate prefilling cost, and the proposed method is simple, training-free, and potentially easy to integrate into existing LLaVA-style systems.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: results are reported on eight image benchmarks, four video benchmarks, and two LLaVA-NeXT model sizes. The method generally improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off over several recent training-free pruning baselines at 25% and 10% token retention.

The two-stage framing is intuitive: first retain a diverse visual subset with greedy k-center selection, then remove remaining visual tokens once cross-modal attention appears low. The ablations suggest that the first stage provides most of the speedup and that the second stage can add modest further gains.
The paper includes useful diagnostic visualizations and ablations over threshold and candidate layer choices, and it acknowledges that training-free pruning adds its own computational overhead.
weaknesses: The originality is limited. Diversity-based visual token pruning and CLS-attention-based selection are already very close to cited concurrent/prior methods such as DivPrune and FasterVLM, while the second-stage removal is closely related to FastV/VTW-style layer pruning. The paper does not convincingly separate its contribution from a straightforward combination of existing ideas.

The second stage, which is central to the claimed novelty, has weak empirical impact. In Table 4, Stage 1 alone already gives nearly all of the benefit; Stage 2 changes performance by about 0.3-0.4 percentage points and only modestly reduces time. Some single-layer Stage 2 settings in Table 6 are slower than the uncompressed baseline, raising questions about overhead and implementation robustness.

The theoretical appendix is not convincing. It assumes orthogonal visual and textual subspaces and then derives independence/covariance results from that assumption, but this assumption is not established for real LVLM embeddings. The proof therefore does not validate the actual pruning criterion or the claimed orthogonality of intra- and cross-modal redundancy.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete and somewhat inconsistent. The abstract emphasizes a 2.6x speedup, while Table 3 reports 1.9x throughput on POPE; Table 4 supports a larger total-time reduction only under a specific evaluation setting. The cost of greedy k-center selection, pairwise similarity computation, attention-ratio computation, and compatibility with FlashAttention-style kernels is not analyzed in enough detail.

Experimental fairness and coverage are concerns. Some baselines are omitted in 13B/video settings due to claimed degradation or modality mismatch, but this weakens comparative evidence. The work evaluates only LLaVA-NeXT backbones, so the claimed architecture-agnostic nature is not strongly demonstrated across modern LVLM families.

Reproducibility details are thin. The paper lacks sufficient implementation details on exact prompts, decoding settings, sampling, token counts for video, runtime measurement protocol, whether reported timings include pruning overhead, and whether baselines were reimplemented under identical optimized kernels.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. For example, the paper claims robust task relevance and broad generalization, but the relevance threshold is manually chosen, evaluated on limited benchmarks, and not tested under long-form generation despite the paper arguing that decoding-stage savings should matter most there.

There are presentation and consistency issues, including typos and numerical/textual mismatches such as the Table 4 discussion referring to incorrect times for the 25% setting. These do not by themselves determine the decision, but they add to concerns about care and reliability.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, training-free, plug-and-play visual token pruning method for LVLM inference. Under the default Algorithms/General framing, the contribution is technically modest but practically meaningful: combining diversity-based token retention with later relevance-based removal is well motivated and easy to integrate into existing LLaVA-style pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall. Results cover LLaVA-NeXT-7B and 13B on eight image benchmarks and four video benchmarks, with consistent gains over several training-free baselines at both 25% and 10% retain ratios. The 10% setting is especially compelling, preserving 95.1% average image performance while improving throughput and reducing memory.

The paper offers useful analysis of why attention-only pruning can fail, including the discussion of positional/attention bias and the observed information migration across decoder layers. The qualitative examples and attention visualizations help make the method’s intuition clear.

The ablations are helpful: Stage 1 provides most of the efficiency gain, Stage 2 adds smaller but consistent improvements, and the threshold/layer-selection studies in the appendix support the chosen design. The method also appears compatible with image and video inputs, which strengthens its practical value.

The manuscript is generally clear, well structured, and reproducibility-relevant details are mostly present, including benchmark descriptions, backbone details, compared methods, pseudocode, hardware, and memory/throughput/FLOP measurements.
weaknesses: Originality is incremental. Greedy k-center selection and attention-threshold-based token removal are natural extensions of existing token pruning ideas; the main value is in a clean combination and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

The evaluation is still centered on a single LVLM family, LLaVA-NeXT. The claims of architecture-agnostic transfer would be stronger with experiments on additional model families with different vision encoders, projectors, or LLM backbones.

Some comparisons are incomplete. FastV and SparseVLM are omitted from the 13B comparison and SparseVLM/GlobalCom2 are omitted from some video settings for plausibility reasons, but this makes the evidence less uniform. It is also unclear whether all baselines were equally tuned for each backbone and modality.

The efficiency story is slightly nuanced. Stage 2 requires attention statistics at selected layers, which may conflict with the strongest form of efficient attention implementations that avoid materializing attention probabilities. The paper claims compatibility with efficient attention operators, but more implementation detail and measured overhead under FlashAttention-style kernels would make this claim more convincing.

The largest advertised decoding-stage benefit is not directly demonstrated on long-generation tasks. Most benchmarks use short answers, and the appendix provides qualitative free-form cases rather than a systematic long-output benchmark, even though the method is expected to be more beneficial as output length grows.

There are minor presentation and consistency issues, such as the ablation text around Table 4 mentioning an apparent incorrect 25% timing value, and the theoretical appendix relies on strong orthogonality/independence assumptions that are more illustrative than persuasive for real LVLM embeddings. These do not undermine the main empirical case but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely efficiency problem for LVLM inference, where visual-token counts dominate prefilling cost, especially for high-resolution images and video inputs.

The proposed ToDRE framework is simple, training-free, and practical: a diversity-based visual-token subset is selected before LLM input, followed by later-layer removal of remaining visual tokens when cross-modal attention becomes small.
The empirical evaluation is broad for this topic, covering eight image benchmarks, four video benchmarks, and multiple LVLM backbones including LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2-8B.

Results are generally consistent: at 10% retention, ToDRE preserves about 95% of LLaVA-NeXT-7B image performance and improves over FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2, and DivPrune; it also shows reasonable transfer to other backbones.
The paper reports practical efficiency metrics, including FLOPs, peak memory, throughput, and total inference time, rather than only accuracy under token retention ratios.
Ablations are useful: the authors isolate Stage 1 and Stage 2, examine retention ratios, layer choice, threshold choice, and pivot selection, which supports the main design choices reasonably well.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental. Stage 1 is closely related to diversity-based pruning such as DivPrune, and Stage 2 resembles prior visual-token withdrawal or late-layer pruning ideas. The main contribution is a useful combination and adaptation rather than a clearly new algorithmic principle.

The claimed theoretical justification is weak. The appendix assumes mutually orthogonal visual and textual subspaces and then derives independence/covariance results from that assumption, but this assumption is not established for actual LVLM embedding spaces and does not convincingly prove that diversity and task relevance are orthogonal in practice.

The empirical gains over the strongest related baseline are modest. For example, at 10% image-token retention, ToDRE improves average normalized performance over DivPrune by about 1.5 points and throughput by only 0.1 samples/s; Stage 2 adds only small gains beyond Stage 1 in the ablation.

The efficiency story is partly overstated. The abstract highlights 2.6x total inference speed-up, while the throughput table reports 1.9x on POPE; the distinction between wall-clock total time, throughput, prefilling-only savings, and decoding savings could be made clearer.

The claim of compatibility with efficient attention operators is not fully demonstrated. Stage 2 requires cross-modal attention probabilities at selected layers, which may conflict with FlashAttention-style kernels unless special implementation details are used; the overhead and implementation path are not described in enough detail.

The evaluation mostly targets short-answer VQA-style benchmarks. Since the paper argues that removing visual tokens during later layers/decoding should especially help longer generation, the lack of quantitative long-form captioning, detailed QA, or grounding-style evaluation leaves an important use case under-tested.

Some design choices appear tuned on the same benchmark family used for reporting, such as the threshold tau and the 7L/8 layer choice. There is limited evidence that these hyperparameters are robust across unseen models, prompts, or tasks.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the paper gives the high-level algorithm and hardware, but does not specify enough implementation details about attention extraction, batching, exact generation settings, prompt templates, or whether all baselines were reimplemented under identical kernels and preprocessing.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the high inference cost of LVLMs caused by large visual-token counts, and it evaluates the proposed pruning strategy on both image and video understanding tasks.

The method is simple and training-free. The two-stage design, retaining diverse visual tokens before the LLM and dropping remaining visual tokens in later decoder layers, is easy to understand and likely straightforward to implement for supported architectures.

The empirical section is reasonably broad, covering LLaVA-NeXT 7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B, eight image benchmarks, and four video benchmarks. The results show consistent accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, especially at 10% token retention.

The ablations isolate the two stages and show that the diversity-based stage provides most of the speedup while the later relevance-based pruning gives a small additional gain. This helps clarify where the benefit comes from.
weaknesses: The originality is limited. The strongest component is essentially a diversity-based greedy token selection scheme, closely related to prior diversity/token-pruning work such as DivPrune. The second stage contributes only marginal gains in the reported ablation, making the overall contribution feel incremental rather than a clearly new algorithmic advance.

The theoretical justification is weak. The claimed orthogonality between intra-modal and cross-modal redundancy is obtained by assuming mutually orthogonal visual/text subspaces and then using an independence lemma that is not convincingly justified for real LVLM embeddings. This reads more like an assumption-driven argument than a meaningful proof supporting the method.

The efficiency claims are somewhat overstated. The abstract emphasizes 2.6x total speedup, but the direct throughput table reports only 1.9x, and the relevance-driven second stage adds only a small runtime improvement after Stage 1. The paper should more carefully distinguish total benchmark runtime, throughput, prefilling cost, decoding cost, and overhead from computing attention ratios.

The claim of compatibility with efficient attention operators is questionable because the second stage requires attention probabilities/ratios. Many optimized attention implementations do not expose full attention maps without extra overhead, and the paper does not adequately quantify or discuss this implementation cost.

The comparison is incomplete or uneven in places. Some baselines are excluded for the 13B setting due to poor transfer, but this makes the comparison less comprehensive. The paper also does not fully analyze sensitivity to model family, prompt style, output length, or high-resolution/video token counts beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

Several improvements over baselines are modest. At 25% retention on images, ToDRE reaches 98.2% average versus 96.6% for DivPrune; at 10%, 95.0% versus 93.5%. These are useful but not large enough to fully offset the limited novelty and weak theory.

The method may be brittle for tasks requiring late or fine-grained visual grounding. Dropping all remaining visual tokens in later layers is plausible for short-answer benchmarks, but the paper provides limited evidence for long-form generation, OCR-heavy reasoning, localization, or cases where visual evidence may need to remain accessible throughout decoding.

Reproducibility details are not fully convincing. Important implementation choices such as exact attention extraction, token ordering after pruning, overhead of greedy selection, hardware/runtime settings, and integration details for Qwen/InternVL are insufficiently specified for reliably reproducing the reported speedups.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely efficiency problem for LVLM inference: visual tokens dominate prefilling cost, especially for high-resolution image and video settings. A training-free, plug-and-play method is practically valuable for computer vision systems.

The central design is sensible: first retain visually diverse tokens in the LLM embedding space, then remove remaining visual tokens in later decoder layers once cross-modal attention becomes small. This separates intra-visual redundancy from task relevance more cleanly than single-score pruning methods.

The experimental coverage is broad. The paper evaluates LLaVA-NeXT 7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2-8B on eight image benchmarks and four video benchmarks, with comparisons to several recent training-free pruning baselines.

The empirical results are consistently favorable. At 10% visual-token retention, ToDRE reports 95.0% normalized average image performance for LLaVA-NeXT-7B, outperforming DivPrune and FasterVLM, while improving throughput and reducing memory. The video results also show good robustness, sometimes matching or exceeding the uncompressed baseline.

The ablations are useful and support the two-stage decomposition: Stage 1 provides most of the acceleration, while Stage 2 gives additional savings and small but consistent performance gains. The pivot, threshold, and layer-selection studies help make the method easier to interpret.
The method is simple enough to reproduce in principle, and the supplementary algorithm gives clear pseudocode for the greedy max-sum token selection.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The first stage is closely related to diversity-based token selection such as DivPrune, and the second stage resembles prior visual-token withdrawal/pruning ideas. The contribution is mainly a well-engineered combination plus empirical validation, not a fundamentally new pruning principle.

The theoretical justification is weak. The claimed orthogonality between intra-modal and cross-modal redundancy relies on an assumed orthogonal subspace decomposition and an independence lemma that are not established for real LVLM embeddings. This does not undermine the empirical method, but the proof overstates what is actually demonstrated.

The claimed contribution of Stage 2 is somewhat limited in practice. The main efficiency gains come from Stage 1; Stage 2 improves total time modestly after token pruning, and the paper itself notes that short-answer benchmarks limit decoding-stage benefits. Stronger evidence on long-form generation workloads would better support the broader efficiency claims.

The adaptive relevance-driven pruning description is slightly confusing. The text claims dynamic layer identification based on attention thresholds, but the implementation appears to check selected late layers around 7L/8, with ablations showing fixed layer choices. The exact runtime policy should be specified more precisely.

Efficiency evaluation is narrower than the accuracy evaluation. FLOPs, memory, and throughput are mainly reported for LLaVA-NeXT-7B on POPE at 10% retention. Since the paper emphasizes practical acceleration and broad compatibility, wall-clock measurements across backbones, video settings, and longer output lengths would strengthen the case.

The greedy diversification step may introduce nontrivial selection overhead for very large visual-token counts, especially video or high-resolution inputs. The paper reports end-to-end gains, but does not isolate or analyze the pruning overhead and scaling behavior in enough detail.

Some baselines are excluded in certain settings due to transferability issues, which may be reasonable, but the comparison would be more convincing if all baselines were carefully tuned or if the exclusion criteria were documented more rigorously.
